corrective.reason: Revision limit reached with one blocker: s11 overgeneralization. End s11 on the quote (or say they pass the same safety approval), without claiming organic pesticides are not regulated more closely.

sentences.text: Dr. Eric Berg puts it in one breath: "what does organic mean it means without pesticides herbicides fungicides and insecticides".

assertions.text: Dr. Eric Berg says organic means without pesticides, herbicides, fungicides and insecticides.

quote.text: what does organic mean it means without pesticides herbicides fungicides and insecticides
quote.speaker: Dr. Eric Berg

sentences.text: So what are organic farmers actually allowed to spray? And if they do spray, does eating organic still keep pesticides out of you?
Dr. Mindy Pelz describes organic produce as "a food that has technically not been sprayed".

assertions.text: Dr. Mindy Pelz describes organic food as a food that has technically not been sprayed.

quote.text: a food that has technically not been sprayed
quote.speaker: Dr. Mindy Pelz

sentences.text: The quickest way to check is to read the rulebook itself.

The US organic regulations say that when a farm's preventive practices are not enough, a biological or botanical substance, or a synthetic one from an approved national list, "may be applied to prevent, suppress, or control pests, weeds, or diseases".

assertions.text: Under the US organic regulations, when preventive practices are insufficient, a biological or botanical substance or a substance on the National List of allowed synthetics may be applied to control pests, weeds or diseases.

quote.text: may be applied to prevent, suppress, or control pests, weeds, or diseases

qualifications: The sentence keeps the rule's condition: only when preventive practices are not enough.

sentences.text: That list is headed "Synthetic substances allowed for use in organic crop production", so not even every synthetic pesticide is off the table. Europe's organic list is no purer: it names paraffin oils, lime sulphur and copper compounds such as Bordeaux mixture.

assertions.text: The US National List is headed synthetic substances allowed for use in organic crop production, so not all synthetic pesticides are banned in US organic farming.

quote.text: Synthetic substances allowed for use in organic crop production

assertions.text: Annex I of the EU organic regulation, the list of plant protection substances authorised in organic production, includes paraffin oils, lime sulphur and copper compounds including Bordeaux mixture.
qualifications: Said as Europe's list; the US examples are not cited, and the pyrethroids-in-traps limit is carried in s17.

sentences.note: s07.a rests on the US heading only; the examples are Europe's, from the EU annex, and the sentence says so. It does not call the EU examples synthetic.

sentences.text: So organic farms do spray. The sharper argument is about whether what they spray is any gentler.
Kurzgesagt tells its viewers, "Organic pesticides are not necessarily safer than conventional ones."

assertions.text: Kurzgesagt says organic pesticides are not necessarily safer than conventional ones.

quote.text: Organic pesticides are not necessarily safer than conventional ones.
quote.speaker: Kurzgesagt

sentences.text: Simnett Nutrition takes the other side: "they're generally not as harmful and they're more closely regulated".

assertions.text: Simnett Nutrition says organic pesticides are generally not as harmful and more closely regulated.

quote.text: they're generally not as harmful and they're more closely regulated
quote.speaker: Simnett Nutrition

sentences.text: A review of organic food and health went through Europe's approved list: of 385 substances authorised as pesticides in the EU, 26 are also approved for organic farming, "evaluated in accordance with the same legal framework".

assertions.text: Of 385 substances authorised as pesticides in the EU, 26 are also approved for use in organic agriculture, evaluated in accordance with the same legal framework as the others.

quote.text: evaluated in accordance with the same legal framework

qualifications: Ends on the quote: the same safety approval, not a claim about how closely organic use is regulated (s17 gives the extra EU conditions).

sentences.text: On the full list, 340 have some identified toxicity, meaning regulators set a safe intake or exposure limit for them; on the organic list, 10 do.

assertions.text: Of all EU-approved pesticide substances, 340 have an identified toxicity (an ADI, ARfD or AOEL assigned), against 10 of those approved for organic farming.
qualifications: s14 says these are hazard classifications of the EU list, not measured exposure.

sentences.note: Identified toxicity is footnote c of the table: an ADI, ARfD or AOEL assigned.

sentences.text: And 27 substances on the full list are classed as "Suspected human carcinogens"; on the organic list, none are, and none is classed as a reproductive toxicant either.

assertions.text: 27 EU-approved pesticide substances are classed as carcinogenicity category 2, suspected human carcinogens, against none of those approved for organic farming, and none of the organic ones is classed as a reproductive toxicant.
qualifications: s14 says these are hazard classifications of the EU list, not measured exposure.

sentences.text: Keep in mind what those tables measure: a substance's built-in hazard, not how much of it reaches anyone, and only for Europe's list, not America's.

assertions.text: The classifications in the review's table relate to a compound's intrinsic hazardous properties, irrespective of its use and exposure pattern, and cover substances approved in the EU.

sentences.note: The limitation for s12 and s13, carried beside them.

sentences.text: The review also names the exceptions. Pyrethrins, an extract of a chrysanthemum, "share the same mechanism of action as the synthetic pyrethroid insecticides".

assertions.text: Pyrethrins, a plant extract from Chrysanthemum cinerariaefolium approved for organic farming, share the same mechanism of action as the synthetic pyrethroid insecticides.

quote.text: share the same mechanism of action as the synthetic pyrethroid insecticides

sentences.text: And copper, a nutrient we all need, is "toxic at high intakes" and a concern for the creatures living in rivers and lakes.

assertions.text: Copper is an essential nutrient, although toxic at high intakes and of ecotoxicological concern due to toxicity to aquatic organisms.

sentences.text: Europe's organic rules even allow a pair of synthetic pyrethroids, but only inside insect traps, where the review judges the risk of them reaching food negligible.

assertions.text: EU organic rules allow the synthetic pyrethroids lambda-cyhalothrin and deltamethrin, but only in certain insect traps.
qualifications: The sentence keeps both limits: EU rules only, and only in insect traps.

assertions.text: The review says pesticides approved for insect traps only have a negligible risk of entering the food chain.

sentences.text: So organic does not mean unsprayed. In America the rules allow listed sprays once prevention has failed; in Europe, where the hazard tables come from, the organic list is mostly of low concern on those tables, with pyrethrins and copper as the real exceptions.

assertions.text: Organic producers may apply listed pest-control substances when preventive practices are insufficient, so organic farming does use pesticides.
Most pesticides approved for EU organic agriculture are of comparatively low toxicological concern, with pyrethrins and copper as the notable exceptions.
qualifications: "on the hazard tables" keeps s14's limit: hazard classes, not exposure.

sentences.note: The question-1 answer; points back to s06 to s17 without re-reading figures.

sentences.text: Which leaves the question most shoppers really care about: if organic farms spray too, does eating organic change what ends up inside you?

sections.name: question-2
sections.title: Does eating organic lower the pesticides in you?

sentences.text: In a DW Documentary film, one interviewee goes further: "the primary advantage of organic produce is that there are no pesticide residues".

assertions.text: DW Documentary says the primary advantage of organic produce is that there are no pesticide residues.

quote.text: the primary advantage of organic produce is that there are no pesticide residues
quote.speaker: DW Documentary

sentences.text: No residues at all? Food testing says otherwise.
Averaged over recent years of European food monitoring, measurable residues within legal limits turned up in 43.7 percent of all samples, and in 13.8 percent of organic ones.

assertions.text: EFSA monitoring, averaged over the last three available years, reports pesticide residues below Maximum Residue Levels in 43.7% of all and 13.8% of organic food samples.
qualifications: The comparison is organic against all samples, not against conventional only, and the sentence says so.

sentences.text: American monitoring data tell the same story from the other side: in the federal Pesticide Data Program, 23 percent of organic samples still tested positive.

assertions.text: PDP data indicated that 23 percent of organic food samples tested positive for pesticide residues.
qualifications: Organic samples frequently contained residues: lower is not none.

sentences.note: "federal" because PDP is the USDA Pesticide Data Program; the passage names it PDP.

sentences.text: A meta-analysis of crop studies puts the gap at residues on 11 percent of organic samples against 46 percent of conventional ones, and an older analysis of American testing programmes found the amounts on organic samples consistently lower too.

assertions.text: A meta-analysis found detectable pesticide residues in 46% of conventional against 11% of organic crop samples.
qualifications: How often residues appeared; s23 says organic samples still carry them.

assertions.text: Baker et al., using USDA PDP, California DPR and Consumers Union data, found residue concentrations in organic samples consistently lower than in conventional ones, crop by crop.
qualifications: "older" carries the verdict's limit that the data are dated; lower, not none (s23).

sentences.text: Residues on food are one thing, though. What actually ends up in your body?
NutritionFacts.org says you can "turn on and off urinary concentrations of pesticide metabolites like a light switch".

assertions.text: NutritionFacts.org says urinary concentrations of pesticide metabolites can be turned on and off like a light switch.

quote.text: turn on and off urinary concentrations of pesticide metabolites like a light switch
quote.speaker: NutritionFacts.org

sentences.text: That sounds like hype, but a systematic review backs it: all four trials it found that swapped people's whole diet to organic and tested their urine, two in children and two in adults, found pesticide breakdown products fell significantly.

assertions.text: All 4 whole-diet crossover trials, 2 in children and 2 in adults, that measured urinary pesticide excretion found a significant difference in pesticide metabolites excreted between the conventional and organic phases.

sentences.text: The drop was often dramatic, as much as 90 percent, and it came within a few days.

assertions.text: The reduction was in most cases dramatic, up to 90% during the organic phase, and occurred within a few days.

sentences.text: What these trials measure is exposure, not health, and a review of farming systems notes that lower residues may not translate into better health outcomes.

assertions.text: Clark and Tilman note that organic foods carry lower pesticide residues, although the difference may not translate into improved human health outcomes.

sentences.note: Paraphrased, not quoted: the passage is a two-column PDF extract.

sentences.text: So yes: eating organic sharply and quickly lowers the pesticides on your food and in your body, but it does not get rid of either entirely, and whether that makes you healthier is a separate question this evidence leaves open.

assertions.text: Switching to an organic diet significantly lowers urinary pesticide metabolites within a few days.
Organic food samples carry residues less often than conventional ones but frequently still contain them.
qualifications: Not entirely: organic samples frequently contained residues.

sentences.note: The question-2 answer; the health limit points back to s29.

sentences.text: Put both answers together and the organic label reads differently.
The answers cover different ground, the field and your body, and the slogan blurs them into a promise the rulebook never makes.
sentences.note: Ties the two answers without re-answering either; the rulebook point was established in s06.

sentences.text: So the next time someone tells you organic means no pesticides, ask the better question: which ones, and how much of them ends up on your plate?
